questions.stem: In a GP clinic, John, 21, tells you he has had loose stools 3 to 4 times a day for 12 weeks, with no blood. He feels tired and his clothes are looser. You want to find out whether he has fat malabsorption. Which question asks about this most directly?
options: "Do you wake up at night needing to open your bowels, or have to rush to the toilet?"
"Does any tummy pain ease after you open your bowels, or come on before you go?"
"What colour is it, and does it float or is it hard to flush?"
"Have you noticed any mucus or slime in your poo or on the toilet paper afterwards?"
questions.why: Pale, bulky, floating, greasy stools that are hard to flush point to steatorrhoea. Patients rarely mention it unless you ask, and it makes IBS unlikely as the explanation.
notes: Night-time diarrhoea suggests an organic cause in general, but it doesn't tell you specifically that fat is not being absorbed.
Pain that eases after opening the bowels is one of the Rome IV criteria for IBS. It doesn't screen for malabsorption.
Mucus points to colonic inflammation or IBS, not to fat malabsorption in the small bowel.

questions.stem: John, 21, comes back to the GP a week later. His tTG-IgA is 210 U/mL (more than 10 times the upper limit), EMA-IgA is positive at 1:320 and total IgA is normal. He has been eating gluten normally throughout. What is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Refer for gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies while he keeps eating gluten
Start a strict gluten-free diet now and repeat tTG-IgA in 6 months to check response
Order HLA-DQ2 and DQ8 typing on a blood sample to confirm the diagnosis outright
Arrange a colonoscopy with terminal ileal and random colonic biopsies under sedation
questions.why: In Australian adults, coeliac disease is still confirmed on duodenal biopsy, even when serology is strongly positive. He must keep eating gluten until the biopsy, because the diet lets the villi heal and can make the histology falsely normal.
notes: The no-biopsy approach is a paediatric pathway. Starting the diet now in an adult would hide the histology and leave the diagnosis unconfirmed.
About a third of the population carries HLA-DQ2 or DQ8. A negative result helps rule coeliac disease out, but a positive one cannot confirm it.
Coeliac disease affects the proximal small bowel. A colonoscopy looks for Crohn's disease or colitis, which are unlikely here.

questions.stem: John, 21, has coeliac disease confirmed by serology. For 12 weeks he has had loose stools that are light coloured and float in the toilet, and he has lost 4 kg. Which mechanism best explains what his stools look like?
options: Blocked bile flow into the duodenum stops bilirubin breakdown products reaching the gut
Autoimmune destruction of the exocrine pancreas stops lipase secretion into the duodenum
Colonic mucosal inflammation causes active secretion of chloride and water into the lumen
Villous atrophy shrinks the absorptive surface, so unabsorbed fat reaches the colon
questions.why: Gluten-driven villous atrophy in the proximal small bowel leaves too little absorptive surface, and the damaged duodenum releases less CCK. Unabsorbed fat makes the stool pale, bulky and floating (steatorrhoea).
notes: Biliary obstruction causes pale stools but also jaundice, dark urine and a cholestatic LFT pattern. John has none of these.
Coeliac disease does not destroy the pancreas. Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency in a young man would suggest cystic fibrosis or chronic pancreatitis.
Colonic inflammation causes watery or bloody diarrhoea with mucus, not pale, fatty, floating stools.

questions.stem: John, 21, has coeliac disease. His bloods show Hb 116 g/L, MCV 74 fL, ferritin 6 microg/L, low folate and a normal B12. Damage to which part of the gut best explains why iron and folate are low while B12 is spared?
options: Terminal ileum and ileocaecal valve region
questions.why: Iron is absorbed mainly in the duodenum and folate in the proximal jejunum. Coeliac disease damages this proximal bowel most, while B12 is absorbed further down, in the terminal ileum.
notes: The terminal ileum absorbs B12 and bile salts. Disease here, such as Crohn's, would lower B12, but John's B12 is normal.
Parietal cells in the gastric body and fundus make intrinsic factor. Losing them, as in pernicious anaemia, would cause B12 deficiency, not this pattern.
The colon absorbs water and electrolytes but plays no real part in absorbing iron or folate.
